title: Could You Cover a $400 Surprise? The Emergency Fund Math, with New Fed Data
title_card: How big should your emergency fund be?
description: Six in ten American adults were hit by a major unexpected expense last year – usually a car, a house repair or a medical bill, typically $1,000 to $2,000. Yet only 63% could cover even $400 with cash. We go through the Federal Reserve's newest data on emergency savings, what a surprise bill costs when it lands on a credit card, how big an emergency fund really needs to be, and how people build one.
sources: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 'Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025' (Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking, SHED, May 2026): $400 emergency expense (63% cash or equivalent, figure 24, 2013–2025; table 25, other ways to pay), largest emergency expense payable from savings (table 26), major unexpected expenses and their amounts (table 23, figure 23), three-month rainy day fund (55%; figure 25 and table 27)

U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Expenditures in 2024 (released December 19, 2025): average annual expenditures per consumer unit $78,535; housing $26,266, transportation $13,318, food $10,169, healthcare $6,197
Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, G.19 Consumer Credit: commercial bank interest rate on credit card plans, all accounts, 21.19% (August 2026)
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), National Rates and Rate Caps: national deposit rate for savings accounts, 0.37% (September 2026)
Illustrative calculations: $1,500 at 21.19% a year, interest added monthly; example minimum payment of 1% of the balance plus interest, at least $25; weekly saving amounts

beats.say: Last year, six in ten American adults got hit by a big bill they didn't see coming. A car repair. A broken boiler. A hospital visit.

show.caption: of US adults had a major unexpected expense in the past year

beats.say: The typical one cost between one and two thousand dollars.
And yet more than a third of adults couldn't cover even four hundred dollars with cash.

show.caption: would not cover a $400 surprise with cash or equivalent

beats.say: Today: the Federal Reserve's newest data on emergency savings, what a surprise bill really costs when you don't have the cash – and how big your emergency fund actually needs to be.
Quick note: this is general information, not financial advice.
Every year, the Federal Reserve asks about twelve thousand Americans the same question: if you had an unexpected expense of four hundred dollars, how would you pay for it?

show.text: An unexpected *$400* expense. How would you pay?
show.source: Federal Reserve, Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking

beats.say: Cash, savings, or a credit card you pay off in full at the next statement counts as passing. Here's the share who pass, since 2013.

show.heading: Would cover a $400 surprise with cash or equivalent
show.sub: Share of US adults, 2013–2025 · Federal Reserve, Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking

beats.say: In 2013, only half of adults.
Then it climbed for eight years straight. In 2021, with pandemic support payments in the bank, it peaked at sixty-eight percent.
Since then it's been stuck. Sixty-three percent in 2022, 2023, 2024 – and again in 2025.
And this isn't about the four hundred dollars getting more expensive. The Fed tested five hundred dollars instead with some people, and the answers barely changed.
So what about the thirty-seven percent who wouldn't pay in cash? Here's what they said they'd do.

show.heading: How the others would pay a $400 surprise
items: Bank loan or line of credit
show.source: Share of all US adults, 2025, more than one answer possible · Federal Reserve, SHED 2025

beats.say: The most common answer: put it on a credit card and pay it off over time. Fifteen percent of all adults.
Ten percent would borrow from friends or family. Seven percent would sell something.
And twelve percent of all adults – about one in eight – said they could not pay it at all. Not by any means.
Ask the question differently – what's the biggest emergency you could pay right now from savings alone? – and eighteen percent said: less than a hundred dollars.

show.caption: could cover less than $100 from savings right now

beats.say: Among adults earning less than fifty thousand dollars a year, four in ten couldn't cover even a hundred-dollar emergency from savings alone. Six in ten couldn't cover five hundred.

show.caption: adults under $50k income who couldn't cover $100 from savings

beats.say: That's not a lack of discipline in most cases. When every dollar has a job before it arrives, there's nothing left to put aside. Which is exactly why the first few hundred dollars matter so much.
And four hundred dollars is a gentle test. Here's what actually hit people in the past twelve months.

show.heading: Major unexpected expenses in the past 12 months
show.source: Share of US adults, 2025 · Federal Reserve, SHED 2025

beats.say: The number one surprise: the car. Thirty percent of adults had a major repair or had to replace a vehicle.
Then a house or appliance repair, twenty-two percent. A major medical bill, twenty-one percent.
For all three of those, the typical bill – the median – was between one thousand and two thousand dollars. Legal bills, taxes and fines ran higher: typically two to five thousand.

show.caption: median cost of a major car, house or medical surprise

beats.say: So the realistic test isn't four hundred dollars. It's more like fifteen hundred. And it doesn't come once in a lifetime – for six in ten people, it came last year.
Now let's see what happens when a fifteen-hundred-dollar car repair lands on a credit card, at the average rate of twenty-one percent.

show.caption: car repair, on a card at 21.19%

beats.say: If you pay only the minimum – with a common formula of one percent plus interest, at least twenty-five dollars – it takes about nine years to clear.
And you pay about sixteen hundred dollars in interest. The repair ends up costing more than twice its price.
Pay a fixed hundred dollars a month instead, and it's gone in a year and a half with about two hundred and sixty dollars of interest. Better – but still money that buys nothing.
And here's the real trap: the next surprise doesn't wait until the last one is paid off. Six in ten people had one last year. Without a cushion, the balances stack.
That's the real job of an emergency fund. Not getting rich. Stopping one bad month from turning into nine years of payments.

show.text: An emergency fund turns a *crisis* into an *inconvenience*.

beats.say: If this already changed how you see that savings account, leave a like – it really helps the channel.
So how much do you actually need? The rule you'll hear most is three months of expenses. Fifty-five percent of adults say they have that.

show.caption: have a rainy day fund for 3 months of expenses, 2025

beats.say: What is three months, in dollars? The average American household spends about seventy-eight thousand five hundred dollars a year. That's about sixty-five hundred a month.

show.caption: average yearly spending per US household, 2024

beats.say: Three months of everything: almost twenty thousand dollars. For a lot of people, that number alone is enough to give up before starting.
But in an emergency, you don't pay for everything. Take just housing, food, transportation and healthcare: about fifty-six thousand a year on average. Three months of that is about fourteen thousand.

show.heading: 3 months of spending, average US household

beats.say: And you don't need it on day one. Think of it in steps. Step one: enough for the typical surprise – about fifteen hundred to two thousand dollars. That alone covers the car, the boiler, the hospital bill.
Step two: one month of essentials. Step three: three months. Each step makes the next surprise smaller.

Your own number depends on your life: how safe your job is, whether you have kids, a car, a house. Someone with a steady income and no dependants may need less. A freelancer or a single earner with a family, more.
Who actually has three months saved? Income matters a lot.

show.heading: Have savings for 3 months of expenses, by income
show.source: Share of US adults, 2025 · Federal Reserve, SHED 2025

beats.say: Under twenty-five thousand dollars a year: twenty-one percent. Over a hundred thousand: seventy-five percent.
Age matters too. Among adults under thirty, thirty-seven percent have three months saved. Among those sixty and older, seventy-one percent. Like net worth, the cushion grows with time.
But the Fed found something that matters even more than income: whether you have money left over at the end of the month.

show.heading: Have a 3-month emergency fund – by money left over each month
show.source: Share of US adults, 2025 · Federal Reserve, SHED 2025

beats.say: Of people who never have money left over, thirteen percent have a three-month fund.
Of people who always have money left over: eighty-six percent.
That's the whole mechanism. An emergency fund isn't built from a windfall. It's built from the gap between what comes in and what goes out – every month.
Here's what small amounts do. Twenty-five dollars a week is fifteen hundred dollars in sixty weeks. Fifty dollars a week gets there in thirty weeks – about seven months.
A common trick: make the transfer automatic on payday, into a separate account you don't see every day. Money you never see is money you don't spend.
One more thing: where the money sits. An emergency fund has a different job from long-term savings, so it follows different rules.

show.source: How emergency funds are usually described – not a product recommendation

beats.say: Safe, because the emergency doesn't wait for the market to recover. Remember: the stock market fell in about one year out of four. That's fine for money you need in twenty years – not for the car repair next month.
Quick to reach, because a surprise bill is due in days, not months. And separate, so it doesn't quietly turn into next month's spending.
But safe doesn't have to mean earning nothing. The FDIC's national average rate on savings accounts is just zero point three seven percent.

show.caption: US national average savings rate, FDIC, Sept 2026

beats.say: On two thousand dollars, that's about seven dollars a year. At an example rate of four percent, it would be eighty. Rates differ a lot between banks and account types – so it's worth checking what yours actually pays.
So, how big should your emergency fund be? Three things from the data.

show.heading: Would cover a $400 surprise with cash or equivalent
show.sub: Share of US adults, 2013–2025 · Federal Reserve, Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking

beats.say: One: surprises are normal. Six in ten adults had a major one last year, typically one to two thousand dollars – and only sixty-three percent could cover even four hundred in cash.
Two: without a cushion, a surprise gets expensive. A fifteen-hundred-dollar repair on a card, paid at the minimum, can take nine years and cost more than twice as much.
Three: build it in steps. First the typical surprise – about two thousand dollars. Then one month. Then three. And it's built from the money left over each month, not from luck.
If you want to understand your money with real numbers, subscribe. And tell me in the comments: what was your last surprise bill?

short.hook: Could you pay a $400 surprise in cash?

beats.say: Quick question. If you got a surprise bill of four hundred dollars tomorrow, could you pay it in cash, or with a card you pay off right away? According to the Federal Reserve, thirty-seven percent of American adults couldn't.

show.caption: would not cover a $400 surprise with cash

beats.say: And four hundred is the easy test. Last year, six in ten adults had a major unexpected expense. The most common one was the car. The typical bill for a car, a house repair or a medical bill: one to two thousand dollars.

show.heading: Major unexpected expenses in the past 12 months
show.source: Share of US adults, 2025 · Federal Reserve, SHED 2025

beats.say: Put a fifteen-hundred-dollar repair on a credit card at twenty-one percent and pay only the minimum each month, and it can take nine years – and cost about thirty-one hundred in total.

The good news: you don't need twenty thousand dollars to start. Fifty dollars a week, set aside automatically, covers the typical surprise in about seven months. How big your emergency fund should really be is in the full video on the channel.
